chapter_title: Deploying Smart Contracts to Testnets and Mainnet

screens.title: Deploying Smart Contracts to Testnets and Mainnet
screens.subtitle: From compiled bytecode to a live contract address on a public network

narration.text: Deploying a smart contract is the moment your code becomes a live program on a blockchain. In this lesson you will learn the full path: compile Solidity into EVM bytecode and an ABI, configure a development framework such as Hardhat to talk to a network provider, and sign and submit a deployment transaction with a secure private key. You will see how node providers like Infura or Alchemy let you reach Sepolia or Mainnet without running a full node. I will also emphasize safe key handling using environment variables and dotenv, and show the small but critical deployment script patterns that perform the bytecode publish step. We’ll use a SimpleStorage example to ground the steps: compile, configure, write the deploy script, fund the account with test ETH, run the deployment command, and confirm the contract address. Finally, you’ll learn common deployment pitfalls such as insufficient gas or wrong constructor arguments, and why testnets are essential practice before any mainnet deployment. By the end you’ll understand what must be prepared and why each step matters for safe, repeatable deployments.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Deployment is the automated transaction that publishes compiled bytecode to a blockchain; configuring your environment, securing keys, and verifying gas and network settings are crucial before you push to a public network.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter — practical deployment skills

narration.text: In this first objective panel we set clear, practical goals. You will understand the lifecycle of a smart contract from development to mainnet, meaning you can explain compilation, bytecode, ABI, and the purpose of a deployment transaction. You will configure deployment tools such as Hardhat or Truffle for multiple networks, configuring RPC URLs and accounts so your scripts run without manual edits. You will learn secure key management, including why private keys must never be hardcoded and how environment variables and dotenv protect secrets. Finally, you will perform a real deployment to a public testnet using an RPC provider. Each objective focuses on a tangible skill: explaining the concept, configuring the environment, keeping credentials safe, and executing a deploy. Practically, this means you’ll run commands, inspect terminal output, and verify the contract address on a block explorer. These skills are essential to move from local testing to real user interaction reliably and safely.

screens.title: The Deployment Lifecycle
screens.subtitle: From source code to immutable on-chain bytecode

narration.text: A deployment lifecycle describes the steps that move a contract from a developer's machine to a live blockchain. First, the contract is compiled: Solidity is translated into EVM bytecode and an ABI is generated. The ABI is the contract's interface; tools like Web3. js and ethers use it to call functions once the contract lives on-chain. Next, a deployment script packages the bytecode, includes any constructor arguments, and prepares a transaction. That transaction must be signed with the deployer's private key and sent to a node. Node providers such as Infura or Alchemy accept the signed transaction and propagate it to the network for mining or block inclusion. After the transaction confirms, the network assigns a contract address and the contract becomes immutable unless you planned an upgrade pattern. A concrete example is compiling a SimpleStorage contract to produce bytecode and ABI, then running a Hardhat script that deploys it with an initial value. A common misconception is that only compilation matters — in reality, configuration of RPC, the signing account, and gas planning are equally important. The takeaway: deployment is a multi-step pipeline where each step must be validated to avoid irreversible mistakes on public networks.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Deployment is the automated publishing of compiled bytecode to a blockchain, producing an address and enabling on-chain interactions.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › The Deployment Lifecycle
Why this matters
From compile to confirmed address
  • Compile: produce bytecode and ABI that the EVM will run.
  • Configure: set the RPC URL and account in your framework.
  • Sign & Send: the deploy transaction must be signed with a private key.
  • Confirm: after mining, the network assigns a contract address.
Example
SimpleStorage compiled with Hardhat yields an ABI and bytecode used in the deploy script to set an initial value.
Misconception
Compilation alone is not enough; the RPC config, signing account, and gas must be correct for a successful deployment.
Lifecycle steps (annotated)
1. Compile
Create bytecode + ABI from Solidity sources.
2. Configure
Add RPC url and account in hardhat.config.js via environment variables.
3. Deploy
Sign and send the deployment transaction to the network via a node provider.
Key Takeaway
Treat deployment as a repeatable pipeline: verify each step before moving from testnet to mainnet.

screens.title: Compilation and the ABI
screens.subtitle: Why bytecode and ABI are both required to deploy and interact

narration.text: Compilation converts Solidity source code into two important artifacts: EVM bytecode and the contract's ABI. Bytecode is the low-level instructions the Ethereum Virtual Machine executes, while the ABI describes the functions, inputs, and return types so libraries like Web3. js or ethers can generate call and transaction data. For deployment, the bytecode is packaged into a transaction that creates a new contract account; the transaction's data field contains the bytecode plus encoded constructor arguments. After deployment, you need the ABI and the contract address to call or read functions. A concrete example is the SimpleStorage contract with a constructor that accepts an initial uint256. The compiler emits the ABI describing the set and get functions and bytecode that includes the constructor. A frequent misconception is that ABI is optional at runtime — it is optional for the chain but essential for clients to form correct calls and decode returned data. The practical tip: keep compiled artifacts in your build folder and reference the ABI in your dApp or deployment scripts so you can call functions immediately after deployment. Compilation and the ABI means bytecode is what runs on-chain; the abi is the interface used by off-chain code to interact with the deployed contract.. In practical terms, why bytecode and abi are both required to deploy and interact. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Compile output
keyIdea.text: Bytecode is what runs on-chain; the ABI is the interface used by off-chain code to interact with the deployed contract.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Compilation and the ABI
What the compiler produces

A compiled contract gives you both the bytecode (the executable payload) and the ABI (a JSON description of functions and events). Both are needed to deploy and interact reliably.

Example: SimpleStorage.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT pragma solidity ^0.8.20; contract SimpleStorage { uint256 public storedData; constructor(uint256 initialData) { storedData = initialData; } function set(uint256 x) public { storedData = x; } function get() public view returns (uint256) { return storedData; } }
ABI purpose
Describes how to encode calls and decode return values for off-chain clients.
Bytecode purpose
The payload sent in the create transaction that becomes the on-chain contract.
Practical tips
  • Keep the build artifacts and ABI checked into the dApp project (not the private keys).
  • Verify constructor args locally before encoding them into a deploy script.
  • Use the ABI to immediately read initial state after deployment.
Key Takeaway

Both bytecode and ABI are produced by compilation; one runs on-chain, the other lets clients interact with the running contract.

screens.title: Node Providers: Infura vs Alchemy (and self-hosted nodes)
screens.subtitle: Choose how your deployment scripts reach the network

narration.text: When deploying, your scripts must talk to an Ethereum node to broadcast signed transactions and read chain state. Running your own full node is possible but resource-intensive; most teams prefer hosted providers such as Infura or Alchemy. These providers give you an RPC URL and an A P I key that you plug into your hardhat. config. js so your deployment script can send transactions without maintaining node infrastructure. The trade-offs are simple: hosted providers are convenient and reliable for development and production deployments, but they introduce a dependency on an external service and require an A P I key stored securely. Running your own node gives you maximal control and privacy but requires maintenance, disk space, and network bandwidth. A common misconception is that hosted providers are insecure by default — when you store RPC keys in environment variables and use secure accounts for signing, hosted providers are a pragmatic default. Example use: set SEPOLIA_RPC_URL to your Infura endpoint in a. env file and reference it in Hardhat to deploy to Sepolia. Ultimately, pick the approach that fits your team's operational capacity and security policy.

keyIdea.title: Node access options
keyIdea.text: Hosted RPC providers simplify deployments but require secure API keys; self-hosting offers control at higher maintenance cost.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Node Providers
Connections you can use
Pick a node access method that fits your team: hosted RPC providers for convenience, or self-hosted nodes for control. Secure the RPC key using environment variables.
Infura / Alchemy
Hosted endpoints that let you broadcast transactions and query chain state using a project key.
Self-hosted node
Run a full node for maximal control and privacy at the cost of maintenance.
Example configuration note
// .env SEPOLIA_RPC_URL="https://sepolia.infura.io/v3/YOUR_INFURA_PROJECT_ID" PRIVATE_KEY="YOUR_PRIVATE_KEY"
Quick checklist
  • Store RPC keys in environment variables.
  • Confirm provider supports your target network (Sepolia vs Mainnet).
  • Monitor rate limits if automating many deployments.
Pro Tip

Use a separate RPC project for deploy tasks to isolate credentials and monitor usage.

screens.title: Hardhat Configuration and dotenv
screens.subtitle: Securely wire RPC URLs and private keys into hardhat.config.js

narration.text: Configuring Hardhat for a network is a small but critical step. The configuration file must reference an RPC URL and the account used for signing. Never place private keys directly in the configuration or commit them to source control. Instead, put secrets into a. env file and load them with dotenv in hardhat. config. js. In practice you define constants such as SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and PRIVATE_KEY in the. env file and reference process. env. SE POLIA_RPC_URL in the config. The deployer account array uses the private key to sign transactions. A concrete example from the chapter shows require of the toolbox and dotenv, reading SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and PRIVATE_KEY, and exporting a networks object with sepolia settings. A common misconception is that environment variables are totally safe if you share the repo; they are not — always add. env to. gitignore and limit access to the file. Finally, validate the configuration by running a simple Hardhat network task before deploying so your script connects correctly and the account address resolves. Hardhat Configuration and dotenv means load rpc urls and private keys from environment variables using dotenv to prevent leaking secrets in version control.. In practical terms, securely wire rpc urls and private keys into hardhat.config.js. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Secure config
keyIdea.text: Load RPC URLs and private keys from environment variables using dotenv to prevent leaking secrets in version control.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Hardhat Configuration
Recommended hardhat.config.js
require("@nomicfoundation/hardhat-toolbox"); require("dotenv").config(); // Load environment variables const SEPOLIA_RPC_URL = process.env.SEPOLIA_RPC_URL; const PRIVATE_KEY = process.env.PRIVATE_KEY; module.exports = { solidity: "0.8.20", networks: { sepolia: { url: SEPOLIA_RPC_URL, accounts: [PRIVATE_KEY] } } };
This setup lets Hardhat use the provided RPC and signing account without exposing secrets in your repo.
.env file (local)
SEPOLIA_RPC_URL="https://sepolia.infura.io/v3/YOUR_INFURA_PROJECT_ID" PRIVATE_KEY="YOUR_ACTUAL_PRIVATE_KEY_HERE"
Remember to add .env to .gitignore. Test connectivity with a simple run of a Hardhat task to ensure the RPC URL and key are correct.
Common Mistake

Do not commit a .env file or hardcode keys — an exposed private key can drain funds on mainnet.

screens.title: Writing a Deployment Script with Hardhat and ethers
screens.subtitle: Automate contract creation and verify state after deploy

narration.text: A deployment script automates sending the compiled bytecode and constructor arguments to the network. Using Hardhat's ethers plugin, you obtain a ContractFactory, call deploy with constructor parameters, wait for the transaction to confirm, and then report the deployed address. In the provided example the script fetches the deployer signer and logs its address, deploys MyToken with an initial supply, awaits confirmation, and logs the deployed address and initial state. This pattern is dependable and repeatable; you can add verification, post-deploy initialization calls, or writes to a registry. A common misconception is that logging the deployer address guarantees success — always await the deployed contract promise and check the returned address. After deployment, use the ABI and contract address to call view functions, such as reading a token balance or the SimpleStorage stored value, to validate the initial state. This immediate verification reduces the risk of silent constructor bugs or incorrect arguments. Writing a Deployment Script with Hardhat and ethers means use ethers contractfactory, deploy with constructor args, await deployment, and immediately validate state to confirm success.. In practical terms, automate contract creation and verify state after deploy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Deploy script pattern
keyIdea.text: Use ethers ContractFactory, deploy with constructor args, await deployment, and immediately validate state to confirm success.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Deployment Script
Typical deploy script (pattern)
async function main() { const [deployer] = await ethers.getSigners(); console.log("Deploying contracts with the account:", deployer.address); const initialSupply = 1000000; // Example constructor argument const MyToken = await ethers.getContractFactory("MyToken"); const myToken = await MyToken.deploy(initialSupply); await myToken.deployed(); console.log("MyToken deployed to:", myToken.address); } main() .then(() => process.exit(0)) .catch((error) => { console.error(error); process.exit(1); });
Note: await the deployed call to ensure the transaction is mined and the address is available for immediate use.
Post-deploy verification
  • Log the deployer address and contract address.
  • Call a view function such as get() or balanceOf to check initial state.
  • Record the address and ABI for your frontend or dApp configuration.
Key Takeaway

Make the deploy script the single source of truth for creating and validating the contract on the target network.

screens.title: Running the Deploy Command and Interpreting Output
screens.subtitle: From terminal command to verified contract address

narration.text: Executing a deployment is done with a single command but has a clear sequence of results you must inspect. The command in Hardhat is npx hardhat run scripts/deploy. js --network sepolia. When you run it the script loads the configured network and environment variables, constructs the contract factory, signs the transaction using the private key, and waits for the transaction to be mined. The terminal will show the deployer address, then the deployed contract address once confirmed. You can also see transaction hashes in the console if your script prints them. After the command finishes, validate the contract by using the ABI and address to call a read-only function; for SimpleStorage, call get() to verify the initial value. A common troubleshooting step when deployment fails is to examine the error: network connection issues often indicate a wrong RPC URL or missing A P I key; insufficient funds errors indicate the deployer account needs test ETH. This immediate verification and error-checking routine turns a single CLI command into a reliable, repeatable deployment practice. Running the Deploy Command and Interpreting Output means run the hardhat deploy command, inspect console logs for deployer and contract addresses, then call a read function to confirm initial state.. In practical terms, from terminal command to verified contract address. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Run & verify
keyIdea.text: Run the Hardhat deploy command, inspect console logs for deployer and contract addresses, then call a read function to confirm initial state.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Run & Interpret
Typical command
npx hardhat run scripts/deploy.js --network sepolia
Watch the console for a printed deployer address, the deployed contract address, and any returned initial state from view calls done in the script.
Misreadings to avoid

A missing contract address usually means await myContract.deployed() did not resolve; ensure the script awaits confirmation and prints the result.

Debug checklist
  • Confirm RPC URL and API key are set in .env.
  • Check the deployer account balance for sufficient test ETH.
  • Review constructor arguments for type and order.
  • Inspect transaction hash on the block explorer for status and gas used.

screens.title: Private Key Management and .env Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Protect the secret that signs your deployment transactions

narration.text: Private keys control funds and the ability to sign transactions. Treat them as the highest-value secret in your deployment workflow. Never hardcode a private key into your configuration or commit it to source control. Use a. env file that is listed in. gitignore, and load keys at runtime with dotenv. If a repository is shared, require contributors to create their own. env file with safe private keys and RPC URLs. Consider hardware wallets or remote signing services for production keys to add protection beyond a plain string in a file. A common misconception is that testnet private keys are throwaway; they still grant control over any testnet funds and reveal signing patterns that could expose errors. For Mainnet deployments, audit who has access to the. env file, rotate keys where feasible, and prefer external signing or multi-signature account setups for high-value contracts. Always validate the public address derived from your PRIVATE_KEY before sending funds or deploying to ensure you are using the intended account. Private Key Management and .env Best Practices means use .env and dotenv for development, and stronger signing solutions for production; never commit private keys to source control.. In practical terms, protect the secret that signs your deployment transactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Protecting keys
keyIdea.text: Use .env and dotenv for development, and stronger signing solutions for production; never commit private keys to source control.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Private Key Management
Recommended practices
  • Store private keys in a local .env file and add .env to .gitignore.
  • Load secrets with dotenv inside hardhat.config.js rather than embedding them.
  • Use separate keys for testnet and mainnet to limit exposure.
Example .env note
PRIVATE_KEY="YOUR_ACTUAL_PRIVATE_KEY_HERE" — keep this file local and private.
Advanced options
  • Use a hardware wallet or remote signer for production deploy keys.
  • Consider multi-signature or timelock patterns for high-value contracts.
  • Rotate and revoke keys if exposure is suspected.
Warning

A leaked private key on mainnet can lead to irreversible asset loss. Treat keys with maximum caution.

screens.title: Gas Fees and the 'Insufficient Funds' Error
screens.subtitle: Diagnose and resolve the most common deployment failure

narration.text: One of the most frequent deployment errors is 'insufficient funds for gas * price + value'. This occurs when the account associated with your private key does not have enough native currency—for Sepolia or Mainnet this is ETH—to pay the gas costs of creating the contract. To resolve it on a testnet, obtain test ETH from a faucet by pasting the deployer address into the faucet UI. On mainnet you must fund the account from a wallet. Another related cause can be an underestimated gas limit or incorrect gas price market assumptions. Hardhat can estimate gas but always check the gas estimate and add a safety margin. A common misconception is that gas is only charged for function calls; in fact, contract creation consumes gas too and can be substantial for complex contracts. As a practical test, check your deployer address balance before running the deployment and log the estimated gas in your script. If deployment still fails, examine the error trace for out-of-gas and confirm constructor logic isn't reverting because of invalid arguments. Gas Fees and the 'Insufficient Funds' Error means ensure the deployer account has sufficient eth for gas, and validate gas estimates before sending the transaction.. In practical terms, diagnose and resolve the most common deployment failure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Gas readiness
keyIdea.text: Ensure the deployer account has sufficient ETH for gas, and validate gas estimates before sending the transaction.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Gas & Troubleshooting
Diagnose insufficient funds
  1. Check the public address derived from your PRIVATE_KEY.
  2. Confirm the balance with a quick RPC call or explorer lookup.
  3. If on Sepolia, use a faucet to request test ETH for that address.
  4. Re-run the deployment once funded.
Pro Tip

Log the deployer balance at the start of your script and optionally halt with a clear error if funds are insufficient.

Gas estimation checklist
  • Use Hardhat's estimate to preview gas usage.
  • Account for constructor complexity — large initial storage costs more gas.
  • Add a margin above estimates to avoid out-of-gas failures during network congestion.

screens.title: Testnet vs Mainnet: Risk and Preparation
screens.subtitle: Why rigorous testnet practice matters before a mainnet push

narration.text: Testnets are essential rehearsal spaces that mirror many behaviors of Mainnet without real financial risk. On a testnet you can deploy repeatedly, test constructor logic, validate gas estimates, and exercise post-deploy interactions until you are confident. Mainnet deployments are permanent and often involve real value, so the stakes are higher: mistakes can lead to lost funds or exposed vulnerabilities. Before any mainnet deployment, thoroughly test on a public testnet such as Sepolia and run unit tests and integration tests locally. A frequent misconception is that passing tests guarantees no mainnet issues; it reduces risk but does not eliminate it. Also consider deploying to a private staging network or multiple testnets to check provider behavior. For mainnet, plan gas budgets, choose secure signing methods, and perform code audits. If you need upgradeability, design and test an upgrade pattern on testnet first. The bottom line: treat testnet deployments as required rehearsals, not optional practice. Testnet vs Mainnet: Risk and Preparation means testnets let you validate behavior cheaply; mainnet requires extra audits, signing safeguards, and careful gas planning because mistakes are irreversible.. In practical terms, why rigorous testnet practice matters before a mainnet push. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Risk contrast
keyIdea.text: Testnets let you validate behavior cheaply; mainnet requires extra audits, signing safeguards, and careful gas planning because mistakes are irreversible.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Testnet vs Mainnet
Testnet benefits
  • Free test ETH from faucets for realistic trials.
  • Safe environment to catch constructor and logic errors.
  • Opportunity to test provider and script behavior under real network conditions.
Mainnet requirements
  • Rigorous audits and automated tests first.
  • Secure key management and possibly hardware or multi-sig signing.
  • Careful gas budgeting and review of immutable behaviors.
Key Takeaway

Always rehearse on testnets and only promote to mainnet after audits, secure signing, and a deployment checklist.

screens.title: Step-by-step: Deploy SimpleStorage to Sepolia
screens.subtitle: A terminal-first flow to complete the assignment

narration.text: Follow a terminal-first sequence to deploy a SimpleStorage contract to Sepolia. Begin by creating a Hardhat project and installing dependencies. Initialize a. env file with SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and PRIVATE_KEY and ensure. env is ignored by version control. Update hardhat. config. js to load dotenv and reference the RPC URL and the accounts array with your private key. Add the SimpleStorage. sol contract to the contracts folder, and write a scripts/deploy. js that deploys SimpleStorage with an initial value such as 42. Fund your deployer address with Sepolia test ETH from a faucet. Run npx hardhat compile to check for compile errors, then run npx hardhat run scripts/deploy. js --network sepolia to perform the deployment. Inspect the terminal output for the deployer and contract addresses, and use the ABI and address to call get() to confirm the initial stored value. If you see insufficient funds, return to the faucet step; if the network fails, verify your RPC URL and A P I key. This repeatable flow gives you a safe, verifiable practice deployment. Step-by-step: Deploy SimpleStorage to Sepolia means a repeatable terminal sequence: setup, .env, compile, fund account, run deploy command, and verify state on-chain.. In practical terms, a terminal-first flow to complete the assignment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hands-on flow
keyIdea.text: A repeatable terminal sequence: setup, .env, compile, fund account, run deploy command, and verify state on-chain.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Hands-on Activity
Deploy SimpleStorage — terminal steps
  1. Initialize Hardhat project and install @nomicfoundation/hardhat-toolbox and dotenv.
  2. Create a .env with SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and PRIVATE_KEY; add .env to .gitignore.
  3. Add SimpleStorage.sol to contracts and write scripts/deploy.js with an initial value like 42.
  4. Fund the deployer address with Sepolia ETH from a faucet and confirm the balance.
  5. Run npx hardhat compile, then npx hardhat run scripts/deploy.js --network sepolia and inspect output for the contract address.
  6. Use the ABI and contract address to call get() and confirm storedData equals the initial value.
Example terminal
You will see the deployer address, a transaction hash while mining, and a confirmed contract address on completion.
Check
If anything fails, verify .env entries, RPC reachability, and that the deployer has enough ETH.

screens.title: Pre-deployment Checklist and Common Mistakes
screens.subtitle: A final review before you push to a public network

narration.text: Before executing a deployment, run a short checklist to reduce risk. First, ensure your contract compiles with no warnings that affect behavior. Then confirm your hardhat. config. js reads RPC and private key values from environment variables and that. env is not committed. Verify the deployer address and that it holds sufficient ETH for gas; on testnet use a faucet. Confirm constructor arguments match expected types and order, and that your deploy script awaits deployed promises. Check the target network in your command line to avoid accidentally deploying to mainnet. If you plan to deploy to mainnet, perform audits, enable external signing or multi-sig for deployer keys, and review gas cost estimates carefully. Common mistakes include insufficient gas, wrong network configs, mismatched constructor parameters, and leaked keys. The final practical habit is to test the entire pipeline on Sepolia, examine the deployed contract address and initial state, and only then prepare for any mainnet promotion. This checklist prevents common, often costly errors. Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Pre-deployment Checklist
Quick pre-deploy checklist
  • Compile succeeds and ABI/bytecode are available.
  • .env contains RPC URL and PRIVATE_KEY and is in .gitignore.
  • Deployer address matches the intended account and has enough ETH.
  • Constructor arguments are correct in type and order.
  • Script awaits myContract.deployed() and logs the resulting address.
  • Test the full flow on Sepolia and verify state before considering mainnet.
Key Takeaway

A short checklist and a testnet rehearsal catch most deployment errors and protect your mainnet assets.

narration.text: These core concepts anchor the deployment workflow. Hardhat or Truffle provide the framework to compile, test, and script deployments. Node providers such as Infura or Alchemy supply the RPC endpoints your scripts use to reach networks without running a local node. Private keys are the critical secret used to sign transactions — keep them out of source control and manage them via environment variables or stronger signing solutions. Commit these ideas to memory and always check them off before you publish any contract to a public network. narration.text: Keep these reminders in mind when you prepare a deployment: always test on Sepolia or another testnet, verify constructor arguments and gas estimates, and confirm the deployer account balance. Maintain a short checklist and automate checks in your deploy script so you catch problems early. After deployment, record the contract address and ABI in your project configuration and verify initial state with a simple read call. These habits make deployments safer and give you confidence when you eventually move to mainnet.
